LanguageData.CC_SetNote_DiplomacyRenown: The colony's houses and the region's are known for what their people did.
LanguageData.CC_Settings_DiplomacyRenown_Tip: Two or more of the colony's people of one family name who are family to each other are a house (twelve at most); the towns' founding families are the region's. A house's renown is read from what its people did that the world saw: contests won at feasts, marriages into other peoples' houses, wards fostered well, seasons abroad as the colony's youth, envoy or hostage, truces sworn as its speaker, the council's business carried abroad; what the peoples remember of them by name (a raiders' camp broken, fighting beside their fighters, trade at their posts, prisoners freed, their wounded tended, and the wrongs); the colony's names for them, years in office and the Empire's titles; notables who think well of them; and the colony's own oaths kept and broken, which each of its houses shares. A deed counts in full for a year, then a tenth less each season down to three tenths. At 10 its name is known in a town nearby, at 30 across the region, at 60 among every people within reach; at -15 it is known for the wrong things. What most of it came from is what it is known for: fighters, healers, hosts, traders, makers or the faithful. Nothing is spent. Notables think up to 15 better of a renowned house's people (up to 10 worse of an infamous one's), good words for them count up to half again, matches with them are offered and accepted up to twice as readily, and what a house is known for draws the world's events of that kind: challengers to fighters, the sick and the hurt to healers, guests to hosts, the far market to traders, work remembered to makers, pilgrims to the faithful, up to three quarters more often; a feast's guests answer a house known for hosting up to three tenths more readily. Off: nothing is told, read or tipped, and the houses kept are kept.
